title: Do Language Models Need Sleep? Offline Recurrence for Improved Online Inference
authors: Sangyun Lee (Carnegie Mellon University; correspondence sangyunl@andrew.cmu.edu)

problem_stated.statement: Scalable memory is not the same as scalable reasoning. The paper claims that attention-SSM hybrid models, whose fixed-size fast weights are supposed to compensate for a bounded attention window, fail not because they run out of storage but because they run out of *computation* for converting evicted context into a usable internal state.
verbatim_anchors: 'However, scalable memory is not the same as scalable reasoning. A fast weight memory may support long-range recall [48], but it is unclear whether it can support deep computation over tokens that are no longer present in the KV cache.' [§1 Introduction, lines 45-47]

'This suggests that the bottleneck is not merely memory capacity as suggested by prior work [32, 2], but the amount of computation available for transforming evicted context into a useful internal state.' [§1 Introduction, lines 49-51]

'we impose a strict context window size as well as a hard-eviction constraint: we clear the context window every 24 tokens' ... 'We impose a prediction-phase latency constraint: during the prediction phase, each answer token is predicted with a single standard forward pass. Extra loops or chain-of-thought tokens are disallowed because they increase prediction latency.' [§4, lines 288-300]
problem_stated.operational_setup: Every C tokens the KV cache is hard-evicted; all information that survives the boundary must already sit in the SSM fast weights; the answer must then be produced in one forward pass with no chain-of-thought. The paper's target quantity is accuracy under this pair of constraints, at a *fixed training-token budget* ([§4 'On task failures', lines 312-317]).

core_mechanism.one_line: At every KV-cache eviction boundary the model runs N extra forward passes over the *same* token chunk, each pass re-writing the SSM fast weights W with keys/values recomputed from the previous pass's features; the KV cache and the refined features are then thrown away and only W crosses the boundary — i.e. (U-W) applied N times over one chunk instead of once, with a learned forward-pass write rule in place of a gradient step.

core_mechanism.what_the_learned_local_rule_actually_upd: The abstract's phrase 'updates the fast weights in its state-space model (SSM) blocks through a learned local rule' [Abstract, lines 24-25] resolves as follows, and the chapter must be precise here because it is the W-path anchor: (1) the OBJECT updated is $W^{(\ell)}$, the matrix-valued fast-weight state of each SSM/GDN/Jet block — nothing else persists across an eviction boundary; (2) the RULE is the block's own gated outer-product write [Eq. 3] (delta-corrected in the GDN runs), i.e. a forward-pass rule whose gates $\alpha_t,\eta_t$ are produced from the token representation by slow weights $\Theta$ — there is no inner loss $\ell$, no $\nabla_W$, and no optimizer state; (3) 'learned' refers to $\Theta$ (the gate producers and projections) being trained by outer-loop backprop through the whole sleep graph, NOT to any test-time learning of the rule; (4) what the sleep adds on top of the ordinary SSM is only the recursion index $j=1..N$ — the same token chunk is written into $W$ $N$ times, with the keys/values regenerated each time from features that depend on the previous $W$. The attention blocks participate in the loop (their KV cache is rebuilt each pass over the chunk) but contribute nothing that survives the boundary.
core_mechanism.relation_to_S0_frame: Reduction to (U-W) with two deviations. (i) The gradient term $-\eta_t\nabla_W\ell(W_{t-1};k_t,v_t)$ is replaced by a learned Hebbian/delta write $+\eta_t v_tk_t^{\top}$ (delta-corrected), and $\beta_tS_{t-1}$ is absent (no momentum). (ii) A recursion index $N$ is added that (U-W) does not have; the canonical rule is a single left-to-right sweep, here it is $N$ sweeps over the same window with regenerated $(k,v)$. The paper contrasts (i) explicitly with the gradient-descent framing: 'Instead of doing gradient descent on predefined losses, our method uses a learned recurrent forward pass to transfer context to weights.' [§2 Context distillation, lines 120-121] and 'our method uses a learned recurrent forward pass as the memory-update rule, allowing more flexible forms of consolidation that need not correspond to a one-step gradient descent on a fixed scalar objective.' [§2 Test-time training, lines 126-128].

update_layer.layers_touched_in_order: One layer only. $\Theta$ moves exclusively in outer-loop training (which is not sleep-time compute under S0 §2.3); $E$ does not exist. There is no cascade and no ordering question.
differences_from_canonical_U_W: The write term is not a gradient. Canonical (U-W) has $S_t=\beta_tS_{t-1}-\eta_t\nabla_W\ell(W_{t-1};k_t,v_t)$; here the write is $+\eta_t v_tk_t^{\top}$ (Mamba-2 form, [Eq. 3]) or the delta-corrected GDN form. The paper defends this choice explicitly against the gradient framing [§2 lines 126-128].

Momentum is absent. In unified terms $S_t\equiv -\eta_t v_tk_t^\top$ with $\beta_t\equiv 0$; there is no persistent momentum buffer. The reserved symbol $S_t$ therefore never appears in its reserved meaning in this chapter — a useful thing to state, since the paper's own $S_t$ means $W_t$.
Retention is a data-dependent scalar/diagonal gate $\alpha_t\in(0,1)$ computed from $x_t$, in the SAME direction as the unified convention (no flip needed, unlike [Titans]).

A NEW index is introduced that (U-W) has no slot for: the pass index $j\in\{1,\dots,N\}$. The update is applied $N$ times over the same token block, and the $(k,v)$ pairs are regenerated at each pass from features that depend on $W^{(n,j-1)}$. So this is not 'more (U-W) steps' — it is (U-W) composed with a feature-refinement fixed-point iteration.

The chunk-start anchor differs from (M4). In chunkwise-parallel training the gradients inside a chunk are all evaluated at the stale snapshot $W_{\xi(t,C)}$; here the recurrence within a pass is the ordinary online SSM recurrence, and the 'snapshot' semantics live at the *pass* level instead: pass $j$ starts from $W^{(n,j-1)}$, which already contains the chunk's content written $j-1$ times.
$W_{\mathrm{init}}=0$ (zero-initialized, [Alg. 1 line 1]) rather than meta-learned. The line's usual load-bearing meta-learned initial state is absent.
update_layer.deviation_from_S0_operational_definition: IMPORTANT AND UNFAVOURABLE TO THE FRAME. S0 §2.3 defines sleep-time compute as computation spent BEFORE the query $q$ arrives. This paper's sleep does not satisfy that in its headline realistic experiment: 'We place the question before the context and exclude Chain-of-Thought traces from the data... This order gives the model the query before it reads the long problem context, allowing it to selectively consolidate information relevant to the question while ignoring filler tokens.' [§6.3, lines 664-667]. The sleep here is query-CONDITIONED and sits on the critical path of a single request; there is no $N_q$ and the amortization equation (A) does not apply. The Depo task is the counter-example inside the same paper: 'the model must form a query-agnostic representation because both $k$ and the start node are randomly sampled for each example' [§6.2, lines 636-637]. The chapter must state both.

new: **sleep duration $N$** — the number of offline recurrent passes performed at an eviction boundary. New reserved symbol for the v2 chapter. [Abstract line 24; §5 line 338]

**consolidation phase vs prediction phase** — a hard partition of the token stream induced by the eviction schedule and, at training time, by the loss mask. 'the consolidation phase (the first 96 tokens...), during which the model must encode context into its fast weights $S_t$; and the prediction phase (the last 4 tokens...)' [§4, lines 294-297]
**hard-eviction constraint** — clearing the KV cache completely every $C$ tokens, as an experimental instrument that makes the fast weight the sole surviving channel. [§4, lines 288-292]

**prediction-phase latency constraint** — the discipline that the answer must come from one forward pass with no loops and no chain-of-thought. This is the paper's real contribution to the frame: it defines what 'wake cost held fixed' means operationally. [§4, lines 298-301]
**offline recurrence for consolidation (as opposed to prediction)** — 'Our key insight is that recurrence can be used not only for prediction but also for memory consolidation.' [§1, lines 70-71]

**reasoning depth at fixed memory load** — the experimental design that separates compute-bound from capacity-bound failure. 'These tasks allow us to vary reasoning demand while holding sequence length fixed, isolating a model's reasoning capability from its information retrieval capability.' [§3.2, lines 242-243]
extended_or_renamed: **fast weights** — used here for the SSM/GDN matrix state, identical in role to the unified $W$; the paper cites the Schlag et al. [49] / Schmidhuber FWP lineage, matching the book's ownership (ch06).

**sleep** — collides with [Sleep] (Behrouz et al., 2606.03979, our $\Theta$-5 chapter). The authors themselves flag the collision in footnote 2: 'This OpenReview submission has a title that overlaps with our original title, namely "Language Models Need Sleep." We were unaware of it when choosing our title and have updated ours to avoid confusion.' [lines 170-172]. The monograph MUST fix distinct short names; recommend [NeedSleep] for this paper and keep [Sleep] for 2606.03979.
**depth recurrence / looped models** — repurposed from prediction-time compute scaling to consolidation-time compute scaling.
contested_or_retired: **'capacity is the SSM bottleneck'** — actively contested. 'Contrary to these works, we show that such models can fail as the required reasoning depth to solve a task increases, even when the amount of information to store is held fixed.' [§2, lines 105-107], against Jelassi et al. [32] and Arora et al. [2].
**meta-learned $W_{\mathrm{init}}$** — not used. The state is zero-initialized [Alg. 1 line 1], unlike [Titans]/[TNT].

inherited_open_question.verdict: The paper does not quote or locate an open question stated by any prior work. It has no 'X asked whether...' sentence anywhere. What it does instead is take prior works' *empirical claims* and contradict their diagnosis.
what_it_implicitly_answers: Jelassi et al. [32] ('Repeat after me: Transformers are better than state space models at copying') and Arora et al. [2] ('Simple linear attention language models balance the recall-throughput tradeoff) attributed the SSM deficit to fixed memory size. This paper implicitly answers 'is capacity the whole story?' with 'no': 'This suggests that the bottleneck is not merely memory capacity as suggested by prior work [32, 2], but the amount of computation available for transforming evicted context into a useful internal state.' [§1, lines 49-51], restated as an explicit contradiction in [§2, lines 105-107].

Allen-Zhu [1] observed on Depo that 'SSMs perform substantially worse than transformers on this task, despite having enough fast weight capacity to store the context' [§6.2, lines 473-474]. This paper supplies a mechanism (insufficient consolidation-time computation) and a fix (offline recurrence), and adopts Allen-Zhu's task and training protocol ($k$ sampled uniformly from $[1,16]$, 'Following Allen-Zhu [1]', §6.2 line 638).

Tandon et al. [55] (end-to-end TTT for long context) perform 'only one gradient step for distilling each context chunk' [§2, line 125]; Zhang et al. [63] 'updates the weights only once per chunk' [§2, lines 133-134]. This paper implicitly answers 'is one update per chunk enough?' with 'no'.

The depth-recurrence line [19, 25, 24, 39, 65] established that more prediction-time recurrence helps. The paper answers a question that line did not pose: whether the recurrence can be moved off the prediction path entirely. 'Unlike previous looped models, our model does not need to loop at prediction time' [§1, lines 76-78].

Noroozizadeh et al. [44], cited at §6.2 line 475, has an open question in its own title ('Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why'). The paper cites it only as support for the 'organizing, not storing' framing and does not claim to answer it.
inherited_open_question.bridge_in_material_for_the_chapter: The honest bridge-in for the W-path chapter is NOT an inherited question but an inherited *misdiagnosis*: the efficient-sequence-model literature (Jelassi [32], Arora [2]) had settled on capacity as the limit, and this paper's contribution is a controlled experiment that separates capacity from computation and shows the second binds first.

open_questions: Training cost and stability of the sleep. 'this gain is not free: during training, we need to perform $N$ deeper forward and backward passes, which can make training slow and unstable. Tackling these challenges is an active topic in recurrent-depth training, with possible approaches including implicit gradients [4] and truncated backpropagation through time [24, 39], as well as various techniques to stabilize training [46, 24].' [§7 Discussion and Limitations, lines 1102-1107] — none of these are attempted in the paper.

Loss of sequence-axis parallelism during training. 'our training is recurrent across context windows... This prevents full parallelization along the sequence axis. However, this loss of sequence-axis parallelism need not hinder wall-clock training time when the window size $L$ is large enough to keep the GPU saturated' [§6.5, lines 1085-1092] — established for $C\in\{1K,2K,4K\}$ at $L=12{,}000$ on one H200 only; behaviour at small $C$ or multi-GPU is open.

Whether the gains survive on tasks that are not inherently sequential. 'Sleep makes training sequential across context and depth dimension, but this sequentiality is also why our method shows gains on the tasks we consider, whose solutions are themselves sequential.' [§7, lines 1108-1110] — an explicit scope limitation from the authors.

Whether the specific fast-weight update rule matters. Declared out of scope: 'the specific update rule does not matter for our discussion' [§3.1, lines 208-209]. No ablation over GDN vs Mamba-2 vs Jet vs delta rule is run, even though the abstract sells 'a learned local rule'.

How to choose $N$, and whether it should be adaptive. $N$ is a fixed hyperparameter per run; adaptive-depth work [25, 21, 50, 5] is cited in related work [§2, lines 137-138] but never applied. No halting criterion, no per-example allocation.

Where the benefit of $N$ saturates. Maximum tested is $N=6$ (Jet only) [§6.3, line 683]; for Ouro, $N$ was capped at 4 for memory reasons ('To keep memory cost during training manageable while using a reasonable batch size', §6.3 lines 681-682), so the saturation point is unmeasured.

Scaling of recurrent depth with model size and training compute. Cited as an open area: 'Detailed analyses of how best to train depth recurrent models suggest the recurrent depth should be scaled with training compute [46, 51]' [§2, lines 139-141]. The paper contributes no scaling law.

Why sliding-window caches under-utilize newly inserted SSM layers, and why hard-eviction warm-up fixes it. 'Analogously to observations in prior work [8], we find that giving the model access to a sliding-window KV cache can make the newly inserted Jet layers underutilized... We find that for $N>1$, using hard eviction for the warm-up stage is crucial for the model to learn to refine the fast weights.' [§6.4, lines 1008-1013] — reported as a recipe, not explained.
Inference-time cost of the sleep. Never measured. The paper measures only training throughput [§6.5, Fig. 6] and never states the serving-time wall clock or the fraction of a session spent asleep.

Whether sleep composes with the mechanisms it cites — context distillation [52, 3, 9, 13], Cartridges [22], TTT gradient updates [55], LoRA-per-chunk [63], or Behrouz et al.'s $\Theta$-path sleep [6]. Every one of these is described in related work and none is run as a baseline or a composition.

Whether training on GSM-Infinite with sleep transfers to other reasoning tasks. The paper motivates GSM-Infinite partly by transfer — 'realistic enough that training on it can improve a model's reasoning capabilities on other tasks [33]' [§6.3, lines 654-655] — but evaluates only in-distribution on its own held-out 1,600 examples.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The headline latency claim is never measured. 'this shifts extra computation to the sleep while preserving the latency of wake-time prediction' [Abstract, lines 25-26] is true by construction of the protocol ('each answer token is predicted with a single standard forward pass', §4 lines 298-299) and is supported by zero timing data. There is no ms/token, no TTFT, no wake-time throughput anywhere. The one throughput figure in the paper is explicitly a TRAINING measurement: 'Training throughput comparison on 1 NVIDIA H200 GPU' [Fig. 6 caption, line 1079].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The paper is sold to a systems audience on a latency property and provides no systems measurement of it — nor of the sleep's own serving cost, which is $N\times$ a full pass at every eviction boundary and lands on the same request.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The transformer failure in the abstract is a tautology, not a result. 'we test our method on ... tasks, on which a regular transformer as well as SSM-attention hybrid models fail' [Abstract, lines 28-29]. But §4 states the reason: 'Under this hard eviction constraint, a standard transformer cannot do better than random guessing as the KV cache has been destroyed before prediction is made.' [§4, lines 302-303]. The transformer has no state that survives the boundary by definition of the setup.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: No full-attention baseline that is allowed to keep its cache is ever run, at any task, at any scale. The reader cannot see how far below an unconstrained transformer the method sits.

unfavorable_facts.fact: No compute-matched baseline. Loops multiply cost roughly linearly in $N$ ('training cost grows roughly linearly with the number of recurrent steps $N$', §6.5 lines 1093-1094), yet every comparison in Figs. 2b, 3, 4 and 5 is at equal TRAINING TOKENS or equal STEPS, not equal FLOPs. At the same x-position, the $N{=}4$ run has consumed roughly 4$\times$ the compute of the $N{=}1$ run.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The central claim — that offline recurrence buys something that ordinary capacity or ordinary compute does not — is never tested against a wider, deeper, or longer-trained non-looped model at matched compute.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Non-monotonicity in $N$ that the paper does not discuss. Fig. 4b (Ouro, op8) prints three values, 0.272 / 0.210 / 0.209, and §6.3 identifies the no-loop baseline as 0.210 and the 4-loop as 0.272 [lines 692-693]; the remaining value 0.209 is therefore the 2-loop run, i.e. 2 loops is marginally BELOW no loop on the hardest operation count. [note-writer's inference from §6.3 prose + Fig. 4b labels; the paper never assigns the third label.]
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The paper's claim is 'increasing sleep duration $N$ improves performance' [Abstract, line 30]; the hardest setting of its most-improved model contains a reversal at $N=2$.

unfavorable_facts.fact: On easy problems more loops are neutral-to-worse. Fig. 4a (Jet): op2 = 0.985/0.985/0.980/0.979, op4 = 0.995/0.994/0.993/0.992 — a spread of 0.6 and 0.3 percentage points respectively across $N\in\{1,2,4,6\}$. Fig. 4b (Ouro): op2 = 0.868/0.863/0.857, op4 = 0.932/0.923/0.903. The paper acknowledges only saturation: 'accuracy often approaches saturation regardless of the number of loops' [§6.3, lines 686-688].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: In serving terms the method spends $N\times$ consolidation compute on every request, but the benefit exists only on the hard tail. The paper offers no mechanism for spending it selectively.

unfavorable_facts.fact: All three evaluation settings are synthetic and at least partly authors' own. The Rule-110 setup (four independent length-24 strings, hard eviction every 24 tokens, first-bit label) is entirely the authors' construction [§4, lines 254-286]. Depo is Allen-Zhu's task but re-parameterized by the authors (75 nodes, $L=360$, $C=75$, left-padding to 300) [§6.2, lines 629-632]. GSM-Infinite is procedurally generated and 'we can generate distinct training and evaluation datasets from the same distribution' [§6.3, lines 655-657] — the eval set is the authors' own 1,600 samples from the same generator. Established long-context benchmarks are named only to be dismissed: 'Unlike retrieval-focused long-context tasks such as RULER [31]...' [§6.3, lines 659-661].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: There is no result on any benchmark the authors did not construct or configure, and no evaluation on natural text at all.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The GSM-Infinite protocol is deliberately non-standard in two ways that both favour the method: the question is placed BEFORE the context, and chain-of-thought is removed. 'We place the question before the context and exclude Chain-of-Thought traces from the data, forcing the model to the final answer in the single prediction time forward pass alone. This order gives the model the query before it reads the long problem context, allowing it to selectively consolidate information relevant to the question while ignoring filler tokens.' [§6.3, lines 664-667].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: Two consequences. (a) The consolidation is query-conditioned, which violates the S0 §2.3 operational definition of sleep-time compute (compute spent before the query arrives) and removes any amortization across queries. (b) Removing CoT removes the standard, strong way of buying reasoning depth at wake time — the very thing the method claims to replace — so the comparison never faces its natural competitor.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Single seed, no error bars, no variance reported. 'For fair comparison, we fix random seeds ensuring that all runs use exactly the same data ordering.' [§6, line 446]. No figure in the paper (Figs. 2–6) shows a confidence interval, a shaded band, or a repeat.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: Several headline gaps are small in absolute terms (Jet op8: 0.351 $\to$ 0.388 = 3.7 points; op6: 0.742 $\to$ 0.812 = 7.0 points) and are unbacked by any variance estimate.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The learning-rate protocol is asymmetric in both directions and is presented as only one of them. 'We tune the Muon learning rate on the $N=1$ model, giving the no-loop baseline an advantage, and use the selected value, 2e-3, for all looped models.' [§6, lines 435-437]. The AdamW lr is simply fixed at 5e-5 with no search [§6, line 433], and §6.3's Muon lr of 1e-3 is inherited from McLeish et al. [39] rather than tuned at all [§6, lines 441-443].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The framing 'giving the baseline an advantage' is defensible, but the same sentence means the treatment arm was never tuned. Since the looped model has a different effective depth, transferring an lr tuned at $N=1$ is a confound in an unknown direction — and it is the only lr protocol used in the two from-scratch experiments.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The equation the paper displays is not the equation it runs, and the paper declines to investigate the difference. Eq. 3 is a Mamba-2-style gated Hebbian rule, but 'In our experiments we use Gated Delta Networks (GDNs), which add a delta-rule correction to this update; however, the specific update rule does not matter for our discussion.' [§3.1, lines 207-209]. In §6.3 a third rule appears (Jet layers, 'dynamic convolution instead of the fixed convolution in GDN', line 438). No ablation over the local rule is run.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The abstract advertises 'a learned local rule' as a component of the contribution; the paper never isolates it, so the reader cannot tell whether the delta correction, the gates, or merely the extra passes are doing the work.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The paper is internally inconsistent about the Depo model. §6 Experiment details says 'we train a 10-layer model from scratch with hidden dimension $d=512$' for Section 6.2 [lines 439-440]; the Figure 3 caption says 'Test loss of a 4-layer GDN-attention hybrid on the $k$-hop knowledge retrieval task' [line 624].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The reader cannot determine which model produced Fig. 3, and the paper has no appendix in which to check.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Depo reports no numbers at all. §6.2 and Fig. 3 give only test-loss curves; no accuracy, no final loss values, no table. And the strongest statement available is that the task is not solved: 'Within our training budget, only the 4-loop model begins to improve on the hardest 16-hop task.' [§6.2, lines 644-645].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: One of three experimental sections contributes no quotable quantity.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The automaton result remains far from solved. Best reported accuracy is 'above 30%' at $N\in\{3,4\}$ against ~10% at $N=1$, after nearly 5B training tokens [§6.1, lines 459-463], on a task whose baseline is explicitly 'close to random guessing'.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The demonstration that sleep helps is real; the demonstration that sleep makes the task tractable is not.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The largest reported relative gain comes from repairing an unusually weak baseline. The 52% op2 improvement in §6.4 runs from 0.596 to 0.905 [Fig. 5, §6.4 lines 1018-1019], but the SAME model (Ouro 1.4B) at op2 under hard eviction with $C=2000$ scores 0.857–0.868 without any loops [Fig. 4b]. The paper itself notes 'this baseline performs poorly even on two-operation problems' [§6.4, lines 1016-1017].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The most striking headline number in the paper measures recovery from a configuration-induced deficit, not a new capability.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The sliding-window result required a bespoke, admittedly fragile two-stage recipe. 'we first warm up only the Jet layers for one epoch and then train the full model for two epochs... We find that for $N>1$, using hard eviction for the warm-up stage is crucial for the model to learn to refine the fast weights.' [§6.4, lines 1009-1013].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The variant closest to a deployable serving configuration (SWA, cache never fully dropped) is the one that does not train without a hand-designed schedule.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Composition with every cited alternative is untested. Context distillation [52, 3, 9, 13], Cartridges [22], in-context autoencoding [23], TTT with real gradient steps [55], per-chunk LoRA [63], and Behrouz et al.'s $\Theta$-path sleep [6] are each described in §2 and none is run as a baseline or combined. The complete comparison set in the paper is $N=1$ versions of the same architecture.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: There is no evidence that offline recurrence beats — or even differs empirically from — the one-gradient-step-per-chunk methods it argues against in §2, lines 122-134.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Scale is far below deployment. Largest models 1.4B/2B, longest task sequence 3,300 tokens, 1–2 H100 GPU-days per run [§6, lines 443-444], $N\le 6$. Ouro's $N$ was capped at 4 purely by training memory: 'To keep memory cost during training manageable while using a reasonable batch size, we use $N=\{1,2,4\}$ for Ouro.' [§6.3, lines 681-682].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The method's cost scales linearly in $N$ and its training memory scales with $N\times$ chunks; the paper is already memory-limited at 1.4B and 3.3k tokens.

unfavorable_facts.fact: Training instability is admitted, not measured or mitigated. 'we need to perform $N$ deeper forward and backward passes, which can make training slow and unstable' [§7, lines 1103-1104]; the proposed remedies (implicit gradients, truncated BPTT, stabilization) are all deferred to future work.
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: The paper offers no evidence about how often the instability bites, and Fig. 2b/3/4/5 are single-seed curves, so instability would be invisible.

unfavorable_facts.fact: The claimed generality of the gain is scoped away by the authors themselves. 'Sleep makes training sequential across context and depth dimension, but this sequentiality is also why our method shows gains on the tasks we consider, whose solutions are themselves sequential.' [§7, lines 1108-1110].
unfavorable_facts.why_it_hurts: By the authors' own account, the three tasks were chosen because they have the property that makes the method work.

decode_cost: PAPER-GROUNDED: the wake-time decode path is byte-for-byte the decode path of the underlying SSM-attention hybrid — one forward pass per answer token, no extra loops, no chain-of-thought tokens [§4 lines 298-300; §1 lines 76-78]. So decode FLOPs/token, decode weight traffic and decode arithmetic intensity are unchanged from the $N=1$ baseline. What changes is only the *content* of the fast weights.

PAPER-GROUNDED: chain-of-thought is removed from the data on purpose [§6.3 lines 664-666], so the comparison the reader should hold in mind is 'N sleep passes at the boundary' versus 'k CoT tokens at decode' — and the paper never runs the second arm.

NOTE-WRITER'S INFERENCE: at serving time the sleep is not free latency, it is *relocated* latency. Every eviction boundary becomes a burst of $N$ full passes over the last $C$ tokens. For GSM-Infinite ($C=2000$, problems 2,000–3,300 tokens, §6.3 lines 663-668) that is roughly 1–2 boundaries per request; for the sliding-window setting ($L\approx4$–$6\times C$, §6.4 line 1007) roughly 4–6 boundaries. With $N=6$ over 14 of 28 Jet blocks [§6.3 line 679], the consolidation FLOPs for a chunk are about $1+ (N-1)\cdot\tfrac{14}{28} = 3.5\times$ a plain prefill of that chunk. The paper reports none of this.
state_bytes_moved: PAPER-GROUNDED: the only state that crosses an eviction boundary is the per-SSM-block fast weight, and it is fixed-size in $t$ [§3.1 lines 204-206]. Everything else — the KV cache and the refined activations — is destroyed [§5 lines 376-382].

PAPER-GROUNDED: peak inference memory for the attention path is capped at the window: 'the active context is still capped at $L$ tokens, as in sliding-window attention (SWA)' [§6.4 lines 703-704]. Windows used: 24, 75, 2000, 512 tokens.

GAP: the paper gives no bytes. It gives $d=256$ / $d=512$ for the from-scratch models [§6 lines 434, 439-440] and layer counts (2 GDN blocks in the 4-layer hybrid; 28 blocks for Jet with 14 looped; 6 inserted Jet layers for Ouro) [§4 line 307, §6.3 lines 677-679], but never the per-block state dimension, head count or dtype. The per-session state size is therefore NOT derivable from this paper alone. Recording as a gap rather than importing GDN defaults.

NOTE-WRITER'S INFERENCE: the traffic pattern is the interesting part regardless of the constant. During a sleep, each SSM block's state is read-modify-written $N\times C$ times instead of $C$ times, on a state that does not grow. So the sleep is a bandwidth-light, compute-heavy burst against a small resident state — the opposite of the KV-cache-bound decode regime the monograph's reader knows. The attention blocks inside the loop, by contrast, re-prefill the same $C$ tokens $N$ times, which IS quadratic-in-$C$ work repeated $N$ times.
batching: PAPER-GROUNDED: training throughput at $N=1$ is essentially unharmed by the cross-window serial dependency when the window is large — 'When window size $L$ is sufficiently large, serialness across context windows do not meaningfully change the throughput compared to the fully parallel baseline' at $C\in\{1K,2K,4K\}$, $L=12{,}000$, one H200, FlashAttention 2 [Fig. 6a caption, lines 1078-1083].

PAPER-GROUNDED: throughput falls roughly as $1/N$ [Fig. 6b caption, line 1081], and $N>1$ required activation checkpointing across the context-chunk axis to avoid OOM [Fig. 6 caption, lines 1082-1083]. Ouro's $N$ was capped at 4 by training memory [§6.3 lines 681-682].

NOTE-WRITER'S INFERENCE (the paper is silent): in serving, eviction boundaries occur at per-request token counts and will not align across a batch. A batch in which one request is asleep and the rest are decoding has two different kernel shapes live at once — an $N$-pass chunked prefill and a batch-1-ish decode step. Either the scheduler stalls the sleeping request's peers, or it must run consolidation as a separate, preemptible job. Nothing in the paper addresses boundary skew, and the paper's only batching remark is that batch size was tuned per setting to optimize GPU utilization [Fig. 6 caption line 1082].

NOTE-WRITER'S INFERENCE: the per-request fast weight already breaks shared-weight batching in the ordinary way (STYLE-NOTATION §3, 'batching' row). The sleep does not make that worse in kind, but it adds a second, bursty phase with a completely different arithmetic intensity.
memory_hierarchy: NOTE-WRITER'S INFERENCE, grounded in the paper's shapes: the sleep partitions cleanly into two very different footprints. (a) The SSM state: small, fixed-size, ideally resident in SRAM across all $N$ passes — this is the part that would benefit from a memory-centric device, since it is read-modify-written $N\times$ per chunk. (b) The chunk's KV cache and activations: $O(C)$ and $O(C^2)$ work respectively, recomputed on every one of the $N$ passes because the features change. At $C=2000$ that is not a small recomputation.

PAPER-GROUNDED CONSEQUENCE FOR CAPACITY PLANNING: because the state is zero-initialized per sequence [Alg. 1 line 1] and nothing persists across requests, this method creates NO per-user or per-session persistent store. It is intra-request consolidation. There is no checkpoint/restore story, no eviction policy for a session cache, and no cross-request amortization — the S0 amortization equation (A) has no $N_q$ to divide by here.

NOTE-WRITER'S EVALUATION for the monograph's spine: this paper is the cleanest available demonstration that the W-path can move compute off the wake path, and simultaneously the clearest demonstration of the W-path's structural limitation relative to the E-path — the E-path's sleep output outlives the request, this one does not.
systems_implications.one_line_for_the_reader: It changes nothing about decode; it adds an $N$-fold chunked-prefill burst at every context-window boundary, whose output is a fixed-size weight state that dies with the request.

cross_path_citations.summary: This W-path paper DOES engage both other paths, but only in single sentences in related work, and never experimentally. Simultaneously it is completely silent on the Titans/Miras/Atlas/TNT/Nested-Learning line — i.e. on the W-path's own dominant research program. Both facts belong in the monograph.

[2]), but it cites NONE of Titans (2501.00663), Miras (2504.13173), Atlas (2505.23735), TNT (2511.07343) or Nested Learning (2512.24695).
own_W_path_silence.why_it_matters: This is the W-path anchor for the v2 monograph, and it does not cite the W-path's own test-time-learning research program at all. Its 'learned local rule' is deliberately positioned as NOT a gradient step [§2, lines 120-121, 126-128] — precisely the position the Titans line takes the opposite side of. So the two halves of the W-path are, in this paper, non-communicating. Record this as a hard S0 §5 finding, not a guess: the bibliography is 65 entries and none of the five is present.

cross_path_citations.verdict_for_the_monograph: Do not report this as 'the paths do not cite each other'. This paper cites the E-path's naming paper and the $\Theta$-path's title-twin, and differentiates itself from both in explicit prose. The accurate finding is narrower and sharper: (i) engagement is uniformly one sentence deep with zero experimental contact — the comparison set in every figure is $N=1$ versions of itself; (ii) the paper is silent on the Titans/Miras/Atlas/TNT/NL branch of its own path, which is a within-path break, not a cross-path one.
